title: The Rich Fool and the Nature of His Loss
english: All his days are in darkness and in mourning and in much anger and sickness and gall (Eccl 5:16). These things can be said about the son, or about both. Again: “And he begot a son, and there is nothing in his hand. Just as he came out naked from his mother’s womb, he will return to go as he came” (Eccl 5:13-14).

Many who possessed the things of “falsely-named knowledge” (1 Tim 6:20) or of Greek philosophy did not have sons who were lovers of these things; rather their sons depart together with them, having acquired nothing in the same way. Many unlearned men, at any rate, have become sons of wise men. This son, then, departs as he came: he came without such instruction and departs without it. But this too is possible: that one begets him who is reputed wise in this way — begets someone in wickedness, in licentiousness, the other kinds of evil — and he comes out naked of what the father was zealous for. The father was zealous, though, not at all about the kinds of evil, but about glory and “falsely-named knowledge.”

He seems somehow, even if […] however these things may remain here. Again: of the father? Not called blameworthily, but at least instead of the praiseworthy he says […]. I say that wisdom is the mother of the wise man: “for wisdom was justified by her children” (Matt 11:19); and the children of wisdom are the wise. “And your mother will guide you” — wisdom. And again, habits — the worse and the better — are called mothers of the things done according to them. So too one is called “son of perdition” (John 17:12), “son of vipers” (Matt 3:7), “of death,” “son of light” (Luke 16:8), and another “son of peace” (Luke 10:6). Here we take the blameworthy mother, since the person under discussion is not an excellent one. According to the anagogy he has a blameworthy mother: just as his mother — wickedness — brought him forth, so he enters here having acquired nothing, in opposition to what his father — who gathered toilsome wealth — provided, and his mother, the habit that bore him.

Here, having acquired nothing, in opposition to what his father had — the one who gathered toilsome wealth — and his mother, the habit that bore him. He will turn back to go as he has come, and he will take nothing of his toil. The fact of the history is clear: he takes nothing of what he labored for. He lets them go and did not know at the time, even if they come upon his enemies. 'He stores up,' he says, 'and does not know for whom he gathers them' (Ps 38:7). And the matter of the upward leading has been said already, that he does not take away anything of what his father and his mother, according to wickedness, make wealthy. Therefore, a praiseworthy mother may also be taken; here she has come to godliness, so that she may possess... [text illegible] ...to enjoy... and indeed this is an evil sickness; for just as it came to be, so it will depart. — Thus it is necessary to take [meaning]: if the entering into a place signifies a local entrance, so also the exiting. For I do not say that the one who entered into this city went out from wickedness, but rather he entered here from another land or city. And what is his abundance, for which he toils toward the wind? His toil becomes wind, that is, his wealth is being overturned by nature; it is not becoming his own, not being held, so as even to be sent to a son. And indeed all his days are in darkness and in mourning. Darkness here means ignorance and the lack of clarity of things. And he mourns, missing those things which he hoped for, from which he thinks he has a pleasant life. And something stands before him. For mourning is raised up over death. In a certain way, therefore, he has died while living, 'and all his days are in darkness and he mourns' (Eccl 5:16). 'And the one who squanders,' he says, 'has died while living' (1 Tim 5:6). If he has died, he is not worthy of being mourned; it is not necessary to raise up mourning over her. For indeed the empty lives living, but he has died, having cast away the life of salvation, the blessed life, as if he had not squandered [it] living according to the human [way].
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
